path.title: Reindeer Herders Cross Continents
path.summary: Permanent land allows Siberian reindeer herding, sled design, and cold-climate clothing techniques to spread gradually into Alaska by foot and caravan. Northern communities on both sides develop a shared seasonal round, exchanging breeding animals and knowledge each year.

path.title: Herders Map Interior River Routes
path.summary: Reindeer sled teams extend seasonal travel inland, producing route maps of Alaskan rivers, passes, and shelter sites shared among northern communities. This exploration is possible because reliable herds, sled designs, and cold-climate clothing from the cross-Beringian exchange reduce the risks of long winter journeys.
path.causalLink: The established cross-continental seasonal round created dependable herds, staging pastures, and guide knowledge that could be extended from coastal Beringia into Alaska's interior.

path.title: Sled Teams Reach Great Slave Lake
path.summary: Guided by the mapped Yukon and Tanana corridors, reindeer caravans reach the Mackenzie basin and Great Slave Lake, recording portages and winter pastures along the way. The journey follows from the parent maps because staged shelter sites and dependable herds turn a previously uncertain interior crossing into a repeatable seasonal route.
path.causalLink: The Fairbanks river-route maps, shelter lists, and staging herds provide the navigational chain and resupply points needed to extend travel eastward into the Mackenzie basin.

branches.title: Caravans Reach Hudson Bay Shores
branches.summary: Reindeer caravans follow lake-and-river portages east from Great Slave Lake and establish a repeatable winter route to Hudson Bay. Reliable draft herds, staged shelters, and pasture knowledge inherited from the Mackenzie journey make the longer crossing feasible without losing animals or supplies.
branches.scene: A line of antlered sled teams crosses a frozen lake at dawn, red marker flags snapping above blue-white ice.
branches.causalLink: Great Slave Lake provides the eastern staging herds, shelter network, and experienced guides needed to attempt the next portage chain toward Hudson Bay.

branches.title: Herders Survey Great Bear Pastures
branches.summary: Herders create a seasonal pasture atlas for Great Bear Lake, marking lichen grounds, wind-sheltered valleys, and safe lake crossings. Systematic rotation follows from the parent arrival because larger resident herds require planned grazing to avoid exhausting slow-growing lichen.
branches.scene: Herders drive small groups between painted pasture markers while ravens circle over a snowfield patterned with winding reindeer tracks.
branches.causalLink: The herds and winter camps established at Great Slave Lake give herders a nearby base from which to survey, test, and rotate lichen pastures around Great Bear Lake.

branches.title: Carved Antler Maps Become Art
branches.summary: Delta carvers incise antler panels with river bends, camps, stars, and herd movements, blending route records with decorative storytelling. The art form grows because caravan traffic supplies abundant antler and continually brings new journeys worth recording.
branches.scene: In a lamplit winter dwelling, a carver turns an antler panel so etched rivers and reindeer catch the light.
branches.causalLink: Regular Mackenzie caravans from Great Slave Lake carry shed antlers, route knowledge, and visiting carvers to delta communities, where those materials can be turned into durable records.
